meaning: Someone or something tends to show a bad habit or tendency. Carries the speaker's criticism.
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + きらいがある; Noun + の + きらいがある

senses.label: Bad tendency
senses.meaning: Like “has a tendency to ...” or “is prone to ...”. Only for bad tendencies, with a critical or disapproving tone. Usually describes long-term character or habits, not one-time events.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + きらいがある (often with 「どうも」, 「とかく」, 「少し」)
examples: He has a habit of exaggerating things.
Young people these days tend not to read books.
That teacher has a tendency to push his opinions on others.

senses.label: Noun + の
senses.meaning: With a noun, add 「の」. Means “there is a hint of ...”. Common phrases: 「独断のきらい」, 「偏見のきらい」. More formal than the verb version.
senses.connection: Noun + の + きらいがある／きらいもある
examples: This report is somewhat overly optimistic.
His judgment tends to be arbitrary.

notes: Only for negative tendencies. ✕「彼は親切にするきらいがある」 does not work.
「きらい」 comes from 「嫌い」, but it is usually written in kana here so it isn't confused with 「嫌い」 (“dislike”).
Mostly used to judge other people or social trends. Used about yourself, it sounds self-mocking.
Don't confuse it with 「好き嫌いがある」 (to be picky / have likes and dislikes).

daily.title: Talking about a friend's personality
daily.description: When discussing a friend's flaw, it softens the criticism.
daily.example: That guy has a habit of blaming everything on other people.

daily.title: Reflecting on yourself
daily.description: Admitting a bad habit of your own, a bit self-mockingly.
daily.example: I have a habit of putting things off.

daily.title: Reading an opinion piece
daily.description: Common in newspaper columns analyzing social trends.
daily.example: Japanese people tend to conform too much to those around them.

work.title: Performance review
work.description: A manager points out a tendency a team member should improve.
work.example: He's very capable, but he tends to take everything on by himself.

work.title: Reviewing a report
work.description: Pointing out that an analysis is one-sided.
work.example: This analysis tends to interpret the data in a convenient way.

etymology: 「きらい」 is 「嫌い」, the noun form of the verb 「嫌う」 (to dislike, to avoid). In older Japanese, 「嫌い」 could also mean “something to be wary of” or “suspicion”. From there it came to mean “a (bad) tendency”.

similar.title: 〜傾向がある
similar.explanation: 「傾向がある」 is a neutral, objective description. It works for good and bad tendencies and is common in statistics and reports. 「きらいがある」 is only for bad tendencies and carries criticism.

similar.title: 〜がち
similar.explanation: 「〜がち」 means “tends to ...” or “often ...”. It is common in speech and writing and can follow nouns (病気がち). 「きらいがある」 is more formal and more critical.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「〜っぽい」 is casual, meaning “-ish” or “quick to ...” (忘れっぽい). 「きらいがある」 is written style and doesn't fit casual chat.

meaning: Something is extreme, “extremely ...” or “... in the extreme”. Mostly used for negative judgments.
connection: Na-adjective stem + 極まる／極まりない

senses.label: 極まりない
senses.meaning: Means “extremely ...” or “utterly ...”. Despite the 「ない」, 「極まりない」 is not a negative. It means “without limit”. Usually follows negative words and shows strong displeasure or condemnation.
senses.connection: Na-adjective stem + 極まりない (失礼, 危険, 不愉快, 無礼, 不親切, 退屈, etc.)
examples: That clerk's attitude was extremely rude.
Driving on a mountain road in the rain is extremely dangerous.
Doing the same task every day is utterly boring.

senses.label: 極まる
senses.meaning: Same meaning as 「極まりない」: “extremely ...”. Sounds stiffer and more formal. Can end a sentence or directly modify a noun.
senses.connection: Na-adjective stem + 極まる (+ noun)
examples: Calling at this hour is utterly inconsiderate.
That was an extremely irresponsible remark.

notes: 「極まりない」 ≈ 「極まる」. It does not mean “not extreme”.
Usually follows two-kanji na-adjectives like 「失礼」, 「危険」, 「迷惑」. Rarely used with i-adjectives.
「感極まる」 (to be overcome with emotion) and 「進退窮まる」 (to be stuck with no way out) are set phrases, not this grammar.
The tone is strong. Said to someone's face it sounds harsh. Mostly used in writing or critical reporting.

daily.title: Complaining about service
daily.description: After bad service at a shop, you complain to your family at home.
daily.example: The way that shop treated us was extremely unpleasant.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Common when news commentary condemns some violation.
daily.example: Tailgating is an extremely dangerous act.

work.title: Complaint letter
work.description: A customer expresses strong dissatisfaction in a complaint letter.
work.example: Your company's response was utterly insincere.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator criticizes a minister's careless remark.
work.example: The minister's remark was extremely careless.

etymology: 「極まる」 originally means “to reach the end / the limit”. 「極まりない」 is the noun 「極まり」 (end, limit) + 「ない」, literally “with no end”, which is why it means “extremely”.

similar.title: 〜の極み
similar.explanation: 「の極み」 follows nouns and is often used for positive feelings (光栄の極み). 「極まる／極まりない」 follows na-adjective stems and is mostly negative.

similar.title: 〜限りだ
similar.explanation: 「限りだ」 expresses the speaker's own feelings (うれしい限りだ) and usually follows emotion adjectives. 「極まりない」 is usually a negative judgment of others or things.

similar.title: 〜ことこの上ない
similar.explanation: 「ことこの上ない」 also means “nothing could be more ...” and works for good and bad. Its form is “adjective + こと + この上ない”. 「極まりない」 leans negative.

meaning: A feeling or state has reached its peak, “the height of ...” or “utmost ...”.

senses.label: Peak of a feeling
senses.meaning: Gratitude, honor, regret and similar feelings are at their highest. Common in formal speeches, thanks and apologies. Very solemn tone.
senses.connection: 光栄, 感激, 痛恨, 恐縮, etc. + の極み (です／でございます)
examples: Receiving such an award is the greatest honor.
Losing in the final is a bitter regret.

senses.label: Peak of a state
senses.meaning: A state has gone to the extreme, “... to the utmost”. Can be positive or negative. Common phrases: 「贅沢の極み」, 「疲労の極み」, 「無責任の極み」.
senses.connection: 贅沢, 疲労, 無責任, 愚, etc. + の極み
examples: Soaking in a hot spring and eating fine food is the height of luxury.
After staying up three nights in a row, I reached the limit of exhaustion.

notes: Only follows nouns, mostly two-kanji words. ✕「うれしいの極み」.
In speeches, 「光栄の極み」, 「感激の極み」 and 「恐縮の極み」 are set phrases.
You can also say 「〜の極みに達する」, “to reach the height of ...”.

daily.title: Enjoying a holiday
daily.description: Half-jokingly exaggerating how much you're enjoying yourself with friends.
daily.example: Drinking beer from the morning is pure bliss, isn't it?

daily.title: Watching sports news
daily.description: An athlete expresses regret in a post-game interview.
daily.example: Making a mistake at the very end is my deepest regret.

work.title: Award speech
work.description: An award winner gives formal thanks at the ceremony.
work.example: I am deeply moved to be congratulated by all of you like this.

work.title: Critical reporting
work.description: An editorial criticizes a company's poor response.
work.example: Trying to cover up the accident can only be called the height of irresponsibility.

etymology: 「極み」 is the noun form of the verb 「極む（極める）」, meaning “end, limit”. The phrase 「〜の極み」 already existed in classical Japanese, as in 「悲しみの極み」.

similar.title: 〜極まる／〜極まりない
similar.explanation: 「極まりない」 follows na-adjective stems and is mostly a negative judgment (失礼極まりない). 「の極み」 follows nouns and is often used for positive feelings (光栄の極み).

similar.title: 〜の至り
similar.explanation: 「の至り」 also means “the utmost ...”, but mostly in set phrases (光栄の至り, 若気の至り). 「若気の至り」 means “the folly of youth” and can't be replaced with 「の極み」.

similar.title: 〜限りだ
similar.explanation: 「限りだ」 follows adjectives and expresses the speaker's own feeling (寂しい限りだ). 「の極み」 follows nouns and is more formal and solemn.

meaning: Something is all one thing from start to finish, “all ...” or “nothing but ...”.
connection: Noun + ずくめ (also written 「づくめ」)

senses.label: All over (appearance)
senses.meaning: From head to toe, everything is the same color or thing. The most typical example is 「黒ずくめ」. An objective description of appearance.
senses.connection: Color noun (黒, 白, etc.) + ずくめ (+ の + noun)
examples: A man dressed all in black came into the shop.
The bride appeared dressed all in white.

senses.label: Nothing but (events)
senses.meaning: Everything happening is of one kind. Common phrases: 「いいことずくめ」, 「結構ずくめ」, 「異例ずくめ」, 「規則ずくめ」. Works for good and bad things.
senses.connection: Noun + ずくめ (だ／の + noun)
examples: This year was nothing but good news, with a promotion and a wedding.
This school is all rules. It's suffocating.
This tournament was full of firsts.

notes: Only works with a limited set of nouns, mostly set phrases: 黒ずくめ, いいことずくめ, 結構ずくめ, ごちそうずくめ, 規則ずくめ, 異例ずくめ.
It means “all”, but without the “dirty / annoyingly many” feel of 「だらけ」.
The official kana spelling is 「ずくめ」, but 「づくめ」 is also common.

daily.title: Describing a suspicious person
daily.description: Telling the police or family what someone was wearing.
daily.example: Someone dressed all in black was standing in front of the house.

daily.title: New Year feasting
daily.description: Describing a holiday table full of good food.
daily.example: New Year's is one feast after another, so I always end up eating too much.

daily.title: Watching sports news
daily.description: Reporting on a season that broke many conventions.
daily.example: A season full of unusual events has finally ended.

work.title: Introducing a new system
work.description: Explaining the benefits of a new policy.
work.example: This system is nothing but good for employees.

work.title: Grumbling about company rules
work.description: Coworkers complaining that there are too many rules.
work.example: Our company is all rules and no freedom.

etymology: Generally thought to come from 「尽くめ」, a form derived from the verb 「尽くす」 (to use up, to exhaust), meaning “all used up, all of it”. So it can be written 「尽くめ」, with the sound voiced to 「ずくめ／づくめ」.

similar.title: 〜だらけ
similar.explanation: 「だらけ」 means “covered in / full of (something dirty or bad)”, as in 「泥だらけ」 or 「間違いだらけ」, with a negative feeling. 「ずくめ」 is more neutral and also works for good things (いいことずくめ).

similar.title: 〜まみれ
similar.explanation: 「まみれ」 means a surface is covered in a liquid or powder (汗まみれ, 血まみれ). 「ずくめ」 is not “smeared with”. It means “all of one kind from start to finish”.

similar.title: 〜尽くし
similar.explanation: 「尽くし」 means “listing everything of a kind”, usually positive (花尽くし, ごちそう尽くし). 「ずくめ」 focuses more on “all the same, nothing but”.

meaning: Something will inevitably cause a result, or the speaker is determined to do something, “cannot fail to ...” or “will definitely ...”.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop ない) + ずにはおかない (する → せずにはおかない); Verb nai-form + ではおかない

senses.label: Inevitably causes
senses.meaning: Something will inevitably make people feel or react a certain way. The subject is usually a thing, such as a work or an event. Often used with the causative: 「〜させずにはおかない」.
senses.connection: Causative verb (nai-form) + ずにはおかない (感動させる, 考えさせる, 不安にさせる, etc.)
examples: This film cannot fail to move its audience.
His remarks are bound to provoke a public backlash.
The incident inevitably made people uneasy.

senses.label: Strong determination
senses.meaning: The speaker's strong will: “I won't let it go. I will definitely ...”. The subject is a person. Forceful tone, often about revenge, holding someone accountable or exposing something.
senses.connection: Volitional verb nai-form + ずにはおかない／ないではおかない
examples: This time I will get to the bottom of it.
I will find the culprit, no matter what.

notes: 「する」 becomes 「せずにはおかない」. ✕「しずにはおかない」.
Written style, rare in conversation. In speech, say something like 「絶対に〜してやる」.
「ずにはいられない」 is about the speaker “not being able to help” doing something. This grammar is about an inevitable effect or refusing to let something go.

daily.title: Reading a book or film review
daily.description: A review praises a work for moving people.
daily.example: This novel cannot fail to stir the reader's heart.

daily.title: Watching a TV drama
daily.description: A character swears revenge.
daily.example: I will have my revenge for this!

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator predicts a policy will cause a strong reaction.
work.example: This tax hike is bound to provoke public discontent.

work.title: Company statement
work.description: A company declares it will fully pursue wrongdoing.
work.example: Anyone involved in the misconduct will be severely punished.

etymology: 「〜ずに」 is the classical negative 「ず」 + 「に」, and 「おく」 means “to leave, to set aside”. Literally, “I won't leave it without doing ...”, hence “will definitely / inevitably”.

similar.title: 〜ずにはいられない
similar.explanation: 「ずにはいられない」 is when the speaker can't control themselves: “can't help ...” (笑わずにはいられない). 「ずにはおかない」 is an inevitable result caused by something, or the subject's strong determination.

similar.title: 〜ずにはすまない
similar.explanation: 「ずにはすまない」 means “it would not be right not to ...” from common sense or social norms. It is about obligation. 「ずにはおかない」 is about an inevitable result or determination.

similar.title: 〜てやまない
similar.explanation: 「てやまない」 means the speaker constantly holds a strong feeling (願ってやまない), usually positive. 「ずにはおかない」 shows an inevitable result or determination.

meaning: Given common sense or the situation, you can't get away without doing something, “must ...” or “it won't do not to ...”.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop ない) + ずにはすまない (する → せずにはすまない); Verb nai-form + ではすまない

senses.label: Morally obliged
senses.meaning: By social norms or common decency, the matter can't be settled unless you do something. Like “it won't do not to ...”. Often about apologizing, compensating or explaining.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ずにはすまない／ないではすまない (謝る, 弁償する, 説明する, etc.)
examples: I broke someone else's things, so I have to pay for them.
After causing this much trouble, you'll have to apologize.
Now that the president knows, I have no choice but to explain the situation.

senses.label: Unavoidable
senses.meaning: Given how things have developed, a bad outcome can't be avoided, “will inevitably ...”. Often with the passive and 「だろう」.
senses.connection: Passive verb, etc. + ずにはすまない (だろう)／ずにはすまされない
examples: After causing such a serious accident, they will surely be held responsible.
This plan simply has to be reconsidered.

notes: 「する」 becomes 「せずにはすまない」. Also written 「ずには済まない」.
「ずにはすまされない」 is stronger: “it can't be allowed to end without ...”.
It is the opposite of 「ずに済む」 (to get by without having to ...). Don't mix them up.
Formal and stiff. In speech, people usually say 「〜しないわけにはいかない」 or 「〜しないとまずい」.

daily.title: After causing trouble
daily.description: A child broke the neighbor's window, and the parents discuss what to do.
daily.example: You broke the neighbor's window, so you have to go apologize.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report says someone may be held responsible.
daily.example: The governor will probably have to resign over this scandal.

work.title: Handling a mistake at work
work.description: Your mistake caused a loss, and you tell a coworker what you plan to do.
work.example: Since I caused such a big loss, I have to report it to the department manager.

work.title: Corporate crisis management
work.description: Management discusses recalling a faulty product.
work.example: This is a safety issue, so we have no choice but to recall the product.

etymology: 「済む」 means “(a matter) is settled”. 「〜ずには済まない」 literally means “the matter won't be settled without doing ...”, hence “you must do it by common sense”.

similar.title: 〜では済まない
similar.explanation: 「では済まない」 follows nouns or 「〜た」 and means “just ... won't be the end of it” (冗談では済まない). 「ずにはすまない」 follows a negated verb: “it won't do not to ...”.

similar.title: 〜ずにはおかない
similar.explanation: 「ずにはおかない」 shows an inevitable result or strong determination. 「ずにはすまない」 focuses on obligation from common sense or the situation.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: 「ざるを得ない」 means “have no choice but to ...” due to circumstances, with a sense of reluctance. 「ずにはすまない」 means “you can't face others unless you do it”, implying social norms.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: 「なければならない」 is the general “must” and the most widely used. 「ずにはすまない」 is more formal and stresses “there's no way to settle things otherwise”.

meaning: Gives an extreme example and implies the rest goes without saying, “even ...”.
connection: Noun (+ particle) + すら; Noun + ですら

senses.label: Even ...
senses.meaning: Gives the most basic, minimal example and implies “never mind anything else”. Usually paired with a negative, with surprise, frustration or exclamation.
senses.connection: Noun + すら (+ negative); Noun + particle (に, と, から, etc.) + すら
examples: I'm so busy I don't even have time to eat.
He couldn't even write his own name.
I couldn't even talk to my parents about this problem.

senses.label: ですら (subject)
senses.meaning: After a subject, use 「ですら」: “even ...”. Usually names an authority or a very capable person to stress how hard or surprising something is.
senses.connection: Noun (person) + ですら
examples: Even experts can't solve this problem.
Even a child knows that.

senses.label: Verb te-form + すら
senses.meaning: After a verb te-form, stresses that not even a minimal action has been done. Common forms: 「〜てすらいない」, 「〜てすらくれない」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + すら + いない／くれない, etc.
examples: He hasn't even apologized yet.
Maybe he's busy, but he won't even read my emails.

notes: Basically the same meaning as 「さえ」, but 「すら」 is more formal and stiff. In casual speech, 「さえ」 or 「も」 is more common.
「すら」 has no “if only ...” use like 「さえ〜ば」. ✕「時間すらあれば」.
Don't confuse it with words like 「すらすら」 (fluently), 「ひたすら」 or 「うっすら」.

daily.title: Complaining about being busy
daily.description: Telling a friend how swamped you've been lately.
daily.example: These days I don't even have time to sleep.

daily.title: Remarking on carelessness
daily.description: Family members talk about someone forgetting the most basic things.
daily.example: That kid even forgot his own birthday.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character who is completely exhausted.
daily.example: She didn't even have the strength left to stand up.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a situation even experts can't predict.
work.example: Even experts find it hard to predict where the economy is headed.

work.title: Complaining about no response
work.description: Reporting to your boss that a client hasn't replied.
work.example: We haven't even received a reply from them.

etymology: 「すら」 is an adverbial particle from ancient Japanese, already found in the Man'yōshū, meaning “even”. From the Heian period on, 「さへ（さえ）」 gradually replaced it, and 「すら」 survives today as a written form.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to 「すら」, but 「さえ」 is more common, works in speech and writing, and also has the 「さえ〜ば」 (“as long as ...”) use. 「すら」 only means “even” and is more formal.

similar.title: 〜まで
similar.explanation: 「まで」 means “even (to that extent)”, mostly in positive sentences, stressing that the range extends to something surprising (子供まで笑った). 「すら」 usually pairs with a negative and gives a minimal example.

similar.title: 〜だに
similar.explanation: 「だに」 is even more old-fashioned than 「すら」, mostly in set phrases like 「微動だにしない」 or 「夢にだに思わない」. 「すら」 is used more widely.

similar.title: 〜だって
similar.explanation: 「だって」 is casual: “even ...” (子供だってわかる). 「すら」 is written style and more formal.

meaning: As soon as something is done, it is undone or happens again, “no sooner ... than ...”. Often with resignation or frustration.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + そばから

senses.label: No sooner done than undone
senses.meaning: Right after the first action, something cancels it out, and this keeps happening. Shows the speaker's resignation or frustration. Used for habitual, repeated situations, not one-time events.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + そばから (often with 「すぐ」 or 「また」)
examples: No sooner do I tidy up than the kids scatter their toys again.
I forget things as soon as I learn them.
As fast as I shovel the snow, it piles up again.

notes: For repeated or habitual things. For a one-time event, use 「〜たとたん」 or 「〜たかと思うと」.
The second part is usually something the speaker doesn't want, with a sense of resignation.
In 「家のそばから」 or 「すぐそばから」, 「そば」 means “near, beside”. That's not this grammar.

daily.title: Complaining about kids
daily.description: A mother complains to a friend that her kids keep messing up the house.
daily.example: As soon as I clean, it gets dirty again. It drives me crazy.

daily.title: Memorizing vocabulary
daily.description: A student sighs that words just won't stick.
daily.example: I forget words as soon as I memorize them.

daily.title: Household budget
daily.description: Lamenting that money never stays in the bank.
daily.example: My salary goes out as soon as it comes in.

work.title: Handling tasks
work.description: Complaining to a coworker that the work never ends.
work.example: As soon as I finish one job, a new request comes in.

work.title: Handling inquiries
work.description: A customer support lead reports on the inquiry load.
work.example: As soon as we answer one inquiry, the next one comes in.

etymology: 「そば」 (側／傍) means “side, nearby”. 「〜そばから」 literally means “starting right beside (what was just done)”, hence “right after doing it, ...”.

similar.title: 〜たとたん
similar.explanation: 「たとたん」 is a one-time “the moment ..., (unexpectedly) ...”. 「そばから」 is for repeated events, and the second part cancels out the first.

similar.title: 〜かと思うと
similar.explanation: 「かと思うと」 means “no sooner ... than ...”, usually describing a single change in someone or something, with surprise. 「そばから」 stresses repetition and frustration.

similar.title: 〜や否や
similar.explanation: 「や否や」 means “as soon as ...”, with two events almost at the same time, for one-time events. 「そばから」 stresses the repeated “it's all for nothing”.

meaning: After a verb, “just ...ing is enough to ...”. After a noun, “not even ...”. An old-fashioned written form.
connection: Verb dictionary form + だに; Noun + だに (+ negative)

senses.label: Just thinking of it ...
senses.meaning: Just imagining or hearing about something brings up a feeling: “just ... is enough to ...”. Usually followed by negative feelings like 「恐ろしい」 or 「ぞっとする」.
senses.connection: 想像する, 考える, 聞く, 思う, etc. + だに + 恐ろしい, etc.
examples: Just imagining being in an accident like that is terrifying.
Just hearing about the war breaks my heart.
Just the thought of another earthquake sends a chill down my spine.

senses.label: Not even ...
senses.meaning: After a noun, paired with a negative: “not even ...”. Mostly in set phrases like 「微動だにしない」, 「一顧だにしない」, 「夢にだに思わない」.
senses.connection: Noun (微動, 一顧, 夢に, etc.) + だに + negative
examples: The soldiers didn't move a muscle.
He didn't give my proposal a second glance.
I never even dreamed I could win the championship.

notes: A written form left over from classical Japanese. Today it is mostly used in set phrases, rarely in freely made sentences.
In the “just ... is enough” meaning, 「だに」 only follows a few verbs, such as 「想像する」, 「考える」, 「聞く」, 「思う」.
The 「だに」 in 「未だに」 (still, even now) is not this grammar.

daily.title: Talking about something scary
daily.description: Friends talk about a close call.
daily.example: Just thinking about what would have happened if I'd fallen is terrifying.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character frozen still with tension.
daily.example: The boy held his breath and didn't move a muscle.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report comments on how serious a disaster is.
work.example: The scale of the damage is terrifying even to imagine.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: Criticizing an authority for ignoring residents.
work.example: The authorities paid no attention at all to the residents' voices.

etymology: 「だに」 is an adverbial particle from ancient Japanese meaning “even” or “at least”. From the Middle Ages on, 「さへ（さえ）」 replaced it, and today it survives only in a few phrases like 「微動だにしない」 and 「想像するだに」.

similar.title: 〜すら
similar.explanation: 「すら」 means “even” and can follow all kinds of nouns freely. 「だに」 is more old-fashioned, mostly in set phrases, and can also mean “just ... is enough to ...”.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: 「さえ」 is the modern everyday “even”. 「だに」 is only used in writing and set phrases.

similar.title: 〜たりとも
similar.explanation: 「たりとも」 follows “一 + counter”, meaning “not even one ...” (一円たりとも). 「だに」 mostly follows fixed nouns like 「微動」 and 「一顧」, or a few verbs.

meaning: Lists a few examples, implying there are more, “... and ... and so on”. Often with complaint or annoyance.
connection: Noun / adjective / verb plain form + だの + ... だの (と)

senses.label: Listing (with complaint)
senses.meaning: Lists two or more examples: “... this, ... that”. Often used to list what others say or demand, with the speaker's annoyance or dissatisfaction. Common in 「〜だのと言う」 and 「〜だのと文句を言う」.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + だの + noun / plain form + だの (と)
examples: My little sister keeps going on about wanting clothes, wanting shoes. So annoying.
The room's too small, the rent's too high... all he does is complain.
I stuffed the fridge full of meat, fish and so on.

senses.label: だのなんだの
senses.meaning: 「〜だのなんだの」 gives just one example and sums up the rest with 「なんだの」: “... and whatnot”. Casual, and also often with complaint.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + だのなんだの (と)
examples: He says he's busy or whatever and never helps out.
With meetings and whatnot, I can't get any rest at all.

notes: 「だの」 directly follows the plain form of nouns, adjectives and verbs. Na-adjectives take the stem or the 「だ」 form.
It has a negative tone, so it sounds rude in formal situations. For neutral listing, use 「〜や〜など」 or 「〜とか〜とか」.
Phrases like 「読んだの？」 or 「死んだのは」 are 「〜んだ + の」, not this grammar.

daily.title: Complaining about a picky kid
daily.description: A mother complains to a friend that her child is a picky eater.
daily.example: My kid says vegetables are too spicy or too bitter and won't eat them.

daily.title: Grumbling about family
daily.description: Complaining that your husband always has excuses not to do housework.
daily.example: My husband says he's tired, he's sleepy, and doesn't do anything.

daily.title: Talking about shopping
daily.description: Talking about all the things you bought when moving.
daily.example: When I moved, I bought all sorts of things, like curtains and dishes.

work.title: Complaining about a difficult client
work.description: Coworkers privately complain about a client's unreasonable demands.
work.example: That client is so demanding: the price is too high, the delivery is too slow...

work.title: Grumbling about work
work.description: Complaining to a coworker after work about too many side tasks.
work.example: Between reports and meetings, I can't get my real work done.

etymology: Generally thought to be the copula 「だ」 + the listing particle 「の」. It came into use for listing from the Edo period on, often with a sense of complaint.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「やら〜やら」 also lists things, but usually means “what with ... and ..., it's all chaos”, stressing how hectic things are. 「だの〜だの」 is mostly for listing others' words or demands, with stronger dissatisfaction.

similar.title: 〜とか〜とか
similar.explanation: 「とか〜とか」 is the general casual way to list things, with a neutral tone. 「だの〜だの」 carries annoyance or dissatisfaction.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: 「たり〜たり」 lists actions with a neutral tone. 「だの〜だの」 can list nouns or things people say, and often carries dissatisfaction.

meaning: Follows “一 + counter” with a negative: “not even one ...”. Stresses that not even the smallest amount is allowed.
connection: 一 + counter + たりとも + negative / prohibition

senses.label: Not even one
senses.meaning: Names the smallest possible amount and stresses “not even a little”. Followed by a negative, a prohibition, or forms like 「〜てはならない」 or 「〜わけにはいかない」. Formal and firm.
senses.connection: 一円, 一日, 一瞬, 一人, 一秒, 一言, etc. + たりとも + negative
examples: Not a single yen of tax money may be wasted.
During a match, you can't let your guard down for even a moment.
I have never forgotten him for a single day.

senses.label: 何人たりとも
senses.meaning: 「何人（なんぴと）たりとも」 is a set phrase meaning “no one, whoever they are”. Very solemn, often seen in notices and declarations.
senses.connection: 何人（なんぴと） + たりとも + negative / prohibition
examples: No one, whoever they may be, may enter this room.
Before the law, no one is an exception.

notes: It basically only follows “一 + counter”. ✕「三円たりとも」.
It must be followed by a negative or prohibition. It can't be used in positive sentences.
Written style. In everyday speech, people say 「一円も」 or 「一日も」.
The 「たりとも」 in 「ふたりとも」 (both people) is not this grammar.

daily.title: A parent warning a child
daily.description: Before an exam, a parent seriously warns their child not to slack off.
daily.example: You can't take even one day off until the entrance exam.

daily.title: Watching a movie
daily.description: A guard protects a forbidden place in a movie.
daily.example: No one shall pass beyond this point.

work.title: Budget meeting
work.description: The finance lead stresses that the budget must not be wasted.
work.example: Our budget is limited, so we can't waste a single yen.

work.title: Safety management
work.description: A site supervisor stresses safety at the morning meeting.
work.example: Please don't let your guard down for even a second while working.

etymology: 「たり」 is a classical copula (like modern 「である」), and 「とも」 is a concessive particle meaning “even if”. Together they literally mean “even if it is ...”, hence “not even one ...”.

similar.title: 〜も (quantity)
similar.explanation: 「一円もない」 and 「一人も来ない」 are everyday expressions. 「たりとも」 means the same but is more formal and firmer.

similar.title: 〜だに
similar.explanation: 「だに」 is also an old-fashioned “even”, mostly in set phrases like 「微動だにしない」. 「たりとも」 only follows “一 + counter” and stresses the smallest amount.

similar.title: 〜すら
similar.explanation: 「すら」 can follow all kinds of nouns to give an extreme example. 「たりとも」 only follows the smallest amount and stresses “not at all”.

meaning: Follows a noun for a role or status: “as a ... (one should ...)”. Stresses behavior worthy of that role.
connection: Noun (role / status) + たる + 者／もの／noun

senses.label: As a ..., one should
senses.meaning: “Anyone in the position of ... should ...”. The second part is usually the proper attitude or action, often with 「べきだ」 or 「なければならない」. Solemn, preachy tone.
senses.connection: Noun + たる + 者（もの）は／もの + 〜べきだ
examples: A teacher must be a role model for students.
A politician should listen to the voice of the people.
A doctor should put the patient's life first.

senses.label: Worthy of / befitting
senses.meaning: Directly modifies a noun, or uses 「たるべき」: “worthy of being ...”, “befitting ...”. Common in 「指導者たるべき人物」 and 「国家たる威信」.
senses.connection: Noun + たる + noun; Noun + たるべき + noun
examples: He's the one who should be our next leader.
One must not lose the dignity befitting a king.

notes: 「たる」 is the attributive form of the classical copula 「たり」, equivalent to 「である」.
The most common form is 「〜たる者（もの）」, used in lecturing or commentary with a solemn tone.
The 「たる」 in taru-adjectives like 「堂々たる」 and 「確固たる」 is not this grammar.
The 「たる」 in 「来たる10日」 (the coming 10th) or 「当たる」 is not this grammar either.

daily.title: A parent lecturing a child
daily.description: A father lectures his child who is about to become a big brother.
daily.example: As the older brother, you need to take care of your little brother.

daily.title: Reading an opinion piece
daily.description: A newspaper column criticizes people who neglect their duties.
daily.example: Parents must not give up on their children's education.

work.title: New employee training
work.description: A trainer stresses the responsibilities of working adults.
work.example: As a working adult, being on time is a given.

work.title: Editorial criticism
work.description: An editorial criticizes the words and actions of top executives.
work.example: A business owner has a responsibility to protect employees' livelihoods.

etymology: 「たる」 is the attributive form of the classical copula 「たり」. 「たり」 came from 「と + あり」 and corresponds to modern 「である」. So 「教師たる者」 means 「教師である者」.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: 「として」 objectively means “as / in the role of ...”. 「たる」 stresses “since you are ..., you should ...”, with a preachy, judging tone.

similar.title: 〜ともなると
similar.explanation: 「ともなると」 means “once you reach the level/stage of ..., naturally ...”, focusing on a change in situation. 「たる」 focuses on the attitude and responsibility a role requires.

similar.title: 〜らしい (typical)
similar.explanation: 「らしい」 means “like a typical ...” (男らしい), describing a quality. 「たる」 is written style and stresses the duty a role demands.

meaning: Concession: “whatever / whoever ...” or “even if it is ...”. The conclusion stays the same.
connection: Noun + であれ; Question word + であれ; Noun + であれ + Noun + であれ

senses.label: Even if it's ...
senses.meaning: “Even if it's ..., still ...”. Accepts a condition, but the conclusion doesn't change. Often paired with 「たとえ」.
senses.connection: (たとえ) Noun + であれ
examples: Even children must follow the rules.
Whatever the reason, violence is not acceptable.

senses.label: Question word + であれ
senses.meaning: After question words like 「何」, 「誰」, 「どこ」: “whatever / whoever / wherever ...”. Similar to 「〜でも」 but more formal.
senses.connection: 何, 誰, どこ, いつ + であれ
examples: Whatever it is, once you start something, see it through.
No matter who the other person is, I won't be rude.

senses.label: Whether A or B
senses.meaning: 「AであれBであれ」 names two opposite or similar examples: “whether A or B, ...”.
senses.connection: Noun A + であれ + Noun B + であれ
examples: We hire capable people, whether they are men or women.
Rain or shine, the game will go ahead as planned.

notes: 「であれ」 is the imperative form of 「である」 used as a concession. Written style. In speech, 「〜でも」 or 「〜にしても」 is more common.
Don't confuse it with 「であれば」 (“if it is ...”).
「〜であろうと」 has a similar meaning with a stronger tone.

daily.title: Teaching kids
daily.description: Parents tell their child to finish what they start.
daily.example: Whatever the job, it's important to take it seriously.

daily.title: Talking about house rules
daily.description: Family members explain that the rules apply to everyone.
daily.example: Adult or child, everyone should keep their promises.

work.title: Company policy
work.description: A manager explains hiring criteria at a meeting.
work.example: Neither nationality nor age will be a hiring condition.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: An editorial condemns discrimination in any form.
work.example: Whatever the reason, discrimination can never be tolerated.

etymology: 「であれ」 is the imperative form of 「である」. In classical Japanese, the imperative could express concession (as in 「さもあれ」, “be that as it may”). So 「〜であれ」 means “let it be ... (the conclusion stays the same)”.

similar.title: 〜であろう
similar.explanation: 「であろう」 by itself is a guess: “probably ...”. For concession, use 「〜であろうと（も）」, which is stronger than 「であれ」.

similar.title: 〜にしろ〜にしろ
similar.explanation: 「にしろ〜にしろ」 also means “whether A or B”, can follow verbs, and is used in conversation too. 「であれ〜であれ」 mostly follows nouns and is more formal.

similar.title: 〜といわず〜といわず
similar.explanation: 「といわず〜といわず」 means “not just A, not just B (everywhere)”, stressing the whole range (手といわず足といわず). 「であれ」 focuses on concession with an unchanged conclusion.

meaning: Ever since a certain event, a greatly changed state has continued, “ever since ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + からというもの (は)

senses.label: Ever since ...
senses.meaning: An event is a turning point, and things have been very different ever since, continuing until now. Carries the speaker's emotion. The second part is usually an ongoing state, not a one-time action.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + からというもの (は), 〜ている／〜ようになった, etc.
examples: Ever since our child was born, my husband comes home early every day.
Ever since he broke up with his girlfriend, he's been down.
Ever since I came to Japan, every day has been one new discovery after another.

notes: The second part must be an ongoing state or repeated action. ✕「日本に来てからというもの、富士山に登った」.
The first part is usually a life-changing event, such as a birth, marriage, illness or move.
It sounds emotional. Usable in speech and writing, but more formal than 「〜てから」.

daily.title: Talking about life changes
daily.description: Telling a friend how life changed after getting a dog.
daily.example: Ever since I got a dog, I go for a walk every morning.

daily.title: Talking about health
daily.description: Telling family your health improved after quitting smoking.
daily.example: Ever since I quit smoking, I've been feeling great.

daily.title: Reading an essay
daily.description: An essayist recalls how things felt after a loved one died.
daily.example: Ever since my mother passed away, the house has been quiet.

work.title: Presenting results
work.description: Explaining the effect of a new system at a meeting.
work.example: Ever since we introduced the new system, work efficiency has gone up dramatically.

work.title: Interview report
work.description: A reporter describes how an athlete's life changed after winning.
work.example: Ever since he won the gold medal, his life has completely changed.

etymology: Made of 「〜てから」 (after ...) + 「というもの」. 「というもの」 means “this whole period of time”, stressing its length and continuity, as in 「この一週間というもの」.

similar.title: 〜て以来
similar.explanation: 「て以来」 also means “ever since ...”, but it sounds more objective and fits plain narration. 「てからというもの」 is more emotional and stresses how big the change was.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: 「てから」 only shows order, and the second part can be a one-time action. With 「てからというもの」, the second part must be an ongoing state.

similar.title: 〜を境に
similar.explanation: 「を境に」 follows nouns and means “with ... as the dividing line (things changed)”, focusing on the turning point itself. 「てからというもの」 follows verbs and focuses on the state continuing afterward.

similar.title: 〜というもの
similar.explanation: 「この一年というもの」 follows a noun for a time span and stresses “this whole period”. 「てからというもの」 follows a verb te-form and stresses “from that event until now”.

meaning: A strong assertion as a rhetorical question: “if this isn't ..., what is?”, meaning “this is truly ...”.
connection: Noun + でなくてなんだろう (か)／でなくてなんであろう

senses.label: Rhetorical assertion
senses.meaning: A rhetorical question that strengthens an assertion: “if this isn't ..., what else could it be?”, meaning “this is without doubt ...”. Very emotional. Common in literature, speeches and commentary. Often used with abstract nouns like 「愛」, 「運命」, 「奇跡」, 「悲劇」.
senses.connection: これが／それが + Noun + でなくてなんだろう (か)／でなくてなんであろう (か)
examples: If this isn't love, what is?
That the two of them could meet again, if that isn't a miracle, what is?
Innocent people lost their lives. If this isn't a tragedy, what is?

notes: A highly emotional written form. Mainly in literature, speeches and commentary. Almost never used in everyday conversation.
The subject is usually marked with 「これが」 or 「それが」.
「なんだろう」 is also written 「何だろう」. For a more formal tone, use 「なんであろう（か）」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel's hero marvels at a fated encounter.
daily.example: Meeting her that day, if that wasn't fate, what was?

daily.title: Watching a sports game
daily.description: A commentator marvels at a miraculous comeback.
daily.example: A huge comeback in the bottom of the ninth! If this isn't a miracle, what is?

work.title: News commentary
work.description: An editorial strongly criticizes the government's poor response.
work.example: What made the damage spread, if not the government's negligence?

work.title: Ceremonial speech
work.description: Praising those who came before at a memorial ceremony.
work.example: The efforts of those who came before us, if this isn't something to be proud of, what is?

etymology: Noun + 「で」 (copula) + 「なくて」 (negative) + 「なんだろう」 (rhetorical question). Literally “if it isn't ..., then what is it?”. By ruling out every other possibility, it strengthens the assertion.

similar.title: 〜にほかならない
similar.explanation: 「にほかならない」 is a direct assertion: “is nothing other than ...”. It sounds rational and is often used to explain causes. 「でなくてなんだろう」 uses a rhetorical question and is more emotional.

similar.title: 〜に相違ない
similar.explanation: 「に相違ない」 is the speaker's confident guess: “must be ...”. 「でなくてなんだろう」 is an emotional assertion, not a guess.

similar.title: 〜と言わずしてなんと言おう
similar.explanation: 「〜と言わずしてなんと言おう」 has a similar meaning: “if we don't call it ..., what can we call it?”. Both are rhetorical emphasis, but this one focuses on what to call something.
